sections.title: Three senders, one cable
sections.narration: Three cameras, three streams, one cable. If the signals share the same path, why don't they become one unreadable mess? The answer depends on a rule that makes combining them reversible.
sections.takeaway: Multiplexing lets independent channels share a physical resource.

sections.title: A medium is not a channel
sections.narration: First separate two ideas. The medium is the physical path; a channel is a way of using that path. One cable can support several channels when the equipment gives their signals distinguishable places or turns.
sections.takeaway: One physical medium can carry multiple logical channels.

sections.title: Combine, carry, separate
sections.narration: At one end, the multiplexer combines the inputs. At the other, the demultiplexer separates them. The important ingredient sits between those names: both ends must agree on exactly how the sharing works.
sections.takeaway: Sharing works only if the receiving end can separate the streams.

sections.title: Read a frequency picture
sections.narration: A wave changes over time. Frequency counts its cycles each second; bandwidth describes a range of frequencies. Shift your attention to the frequency view: it shows where each signal occupies part of that range.
sections.takeaway: A frequency plot shows where signal energy is allocated.

sections.title: Give every stream a band
sections.narration: Place each stream in a different frequency band. Now all three can travel at once because their assigned bands differ. Frequency division makes simultaneous sharing possible by separating signals along the frequency axis.
sections.takeaway: FDM separates simultaneously active channels in frequency.

sections.title: Leave room between neighbors
sections.narration: Why leave gaps between the bands? Real filters have gradual edges, so neighboring signals could interfere. Guard bands provide space between them. The price of cleaner separation is spectrum that carries no channel here.
sections.takeaway: Guard bands trade usable spectrum for easier channel separation.

sections.title: Filter at the receiver
sections.narration: At the receiver, select the green band. A bandpass filter passes that range and reduces others. The green stream doesn't wait for the rest to finish; the receiver separates it by frequency while they coexist.
sections.takeaway: A receiver can extract one frequency allocation with suitable filtering.

sections.title: Work an FDM allocation
sections.narration: Three bands need twenty kilohertz each. Two gaps need five each. Add the occupied widths: twenty, five, twenty, five, twenty. Seventy kilohertz covers this arrangement, before any extra margins at the outer edges.
sections.takeaway: Three 20 kHz channels plus two 5 kHz gaps need 70 kHz.

sections.title: What happens when one is idle?
sections.narration: Now one camera goes quiet. Its reserved band stays empty while the others keep their allocations. The same clear separation that makes this scheme simple can leave capacity unused when traffic becomes uneven.
sections.takeaway: A fixed allocation can waste capacity when its owner has nothing to send.

sections.title: Now divide the time axis
sections.narration: Instead of separating streams by frequency, separate them by time. Let each source use the shared path during an assigned turn. The receiver identifies the source by when its data appears in the schedule.
sections.takeaway: TDM distinguishes channels by when they transmit.

sections.title: Assign repeating time slots
sections.narration: Follow the order: A, B, C, then repeat. The combined stream alternates between sources, and the receiver reconstructs three outputs from those positions. What looks mixed in transit becomes separate again by following the schedule.
sections.takeaway: Synchronous TDM gives channels scheduled opportunities to transmit.

sections.title: Understand a TDM frame
sections.narration: One complete round of slots forms a TDM frame in this example. Here, frame means a repeating timing group. The same word appears elsewhere in networking with other meanings, so keep this particular structure in view.
bullets: A frame contains one slot cycle
Frame here means a TDM cycle
sections.takeaway: A TDM frame groups the slots in one repeated schedule.

sections.title: Keep the schedule aligned
sections.narration: The schedule only works if both ends agree on its boundaries. Shift the receiver's timing and it assigns data to the wrong source. Synchronization is part of the sharing mechanism, not an optional finishing touch.
bullets: Sender and receiver agree on slots
sections.takeaway: Slot timing must be understood at both ends.

sections.title: Work a TDM rate example
sections.narration: Each camera produces two megabits per second. Together they require six megabits per second of useful shared capacity. A practical link needs room for synchronization and other overhead too; useful data isn't the whole transmitted stream.
sections.takeaway: Three continuous 2 Mb/s streams require 6 Mb/s of useful link capacity.

sections.title: The empty-slot problem
sections.narration: When B has no data, its assigned turn still arrives. That empty slot reveals the weakness of a fixed schedule: capacity can go unused even while other sources have work waiting to be sent.
sections.takeaway: Fixed TDM can leave a slot idle even when another input has data.

sections.title: Allocate turns on demand
sections.narration: Give turns only to sources with data, and those empty positions can disappear. That's statistical TDM. The receiver now needs identifiers or equivalent shared information, since a fixed repeating order no longer tells the whole story.
bullets: Labels or state identify the source
sections.takeaway: Statistical sharing adapts to demand but needs coordination.

sections.title: Move from copper to fiber
sections.narration: Change the medium to fiber. Several optical channels can share a strand, represented here by different colors. The drawing tracks their identities; real systems select particular optical wavelengths rather than relying on our display colors.
sections.takeaway: Optical fiber supports channels carried on distinct wavelengths.

sections.title: Combine different wavelengths
sections.narration: Wavelength division carries those optical channels together using different wavelengths. They travel simultaneously through the same fiber. The sharing resembles frequency separation, now implemented with light and the optical equipment needed to handle it.
sections.takeaway: WDM combines distinct wavelength channels on a fiber.

sections.title: Separate the light again
sections.narration: At the far end, optical components separate the combined wavelengths into their outputs. Without that final separation, combining channels wouldn't help. The receiver completes the rule that made sharing one strand useful.
sections.takeaway: An optical demultiplexer separates wavelength channels at the destination.

sections.title: Work a WDM capacity example
sections.narration: Four channels at ten gigabits per second each produce forty gigabits per second of raw combined rate. The multiplication is simple; interpreting it matters. Application throughput can be lower after the system's overhead is included.
sections.takeaway: Four independent 10 Gb/s channels total 40 Gb/s before overhead.

sections.title: Sharing has physical limits
sections.narration: More channels don't remove the limits of the medium. Light can weaken, pulses can spread, and noise can disrupt recovery. Multiplexing organizes available resources; it doesn't create an unlimited, perfectly clean connection.
sections.takeaway: Multiplexing organizes existing resources; it does not remove physical constraints.

sections.title: Compare the three schemes
sections.narration: Compare the pictures. FDM separates frequency bands; TDM separates time slots; WDM separates optical wavelengths. Each gives the receiver a different clue for reconstructing the original inputs after they shared a path.
sections.takeaway: Ask which dimension separates the channels.

sections.title: Choose with the traffic in mind
sections.narration: The right arrangement depends on the traffic. Steady streams may fit fixed allocations, while bursts benefit from serving active sources. Equipment and physical constraints matter too. There isn't one sharing rule that wins in every setting.
sections.takeaway: The useful choice depends on the medium, traffic, and coordination costs.

sections.title: Retell the separation rule
sections.narration: The three cameras never needed three separate cables. They needed a separation rule both ends understood. Remember the bands, turns, and wavelengths: sharing works when the receiver can still tell which information belongs to whom.
sections.takeaway: One cable can support several streams when their channels remain distinguishable.
